page_checks.summary: Selected prepositions are lexically licensed, unlike free spatial prepositions; a particle may precede a simple object; verbal idioms need not be syntactic constituents.
Idioms can license their own subordinate complements, and the book avoids treating traditional phrasal verbs as single verb constituents.
Mobile selected prepositions permit PP-fronting, unlike fixed idiomatic prepositions such as come across in the encounter sense.
Coordination, adverb insertion, and prepositional-passive contrasts distinguish mobile and fixed selections; passivisation is not a universal test.
Fixedness does not force verb+preposition rebracketing; six selected-preposition complementation patterns are classified.
Structure I selects one PP; structure II selects direct object plus PP; source tables mark fossilisation and restricted passives.
Structure II supply alternation differs from give ditransitive; structure III has two PPs, IV selected predicative, V an object and selected predicative.
Structure VI has a PP-object predicand of an as-PC; particle defined by position before a simple NP object, with heaviness caveat.
Intransitive prepositions function as particles; transitive PPs and particles differ in object attachment, order, weak pronoun placement, and AmE out variation.
Fronting, coordination and manner-adverb insertion distinguish transitive PPs from nonconstituent particle+object sequences; same forms can express different senses.
Through/over alternation can be a transitive PP versus NP+intransitive PP, not a particle; contextual omission of locative dependents begins idiom discussion.
Recoverable spatial dependents, seven take in senses and lexicalized aspectual/iterative/durative particle meanings.
Fossilisation can restrict fronting, adverb insertion and object-particle alternation, with sense-specific doubtful variants.
Idiom turn off requires object-before-particle for figurative repulsion; seven intransitive-preposition idiom complementation patterns.
Two-object particle placement has three possible positions but depends on NP length and weak pronouns; look forward to has two separate PPs.
Verb object and PP object have different passive behaviour in mixed idioms; optional as-marked PCs and four verb+NP+transitive-preposition passive classes.
Verbal idioms differ in ordinary/prepositional/both/no passive; fixed PP heads and noun-modifier degrees affect acceptability.
Adjectives can be PCs or particles, some verb+verb idioms are complex predicates, and light uses of verbs contribute little semantic content.
Light-verb constructions contrast with ordinary-verb readings, allow noun modifiers, and quantify products versus acts differently.
Light have can change partitivity and event purpose; light-verb postnominal PP attachment to noun or verb may both be valid.
